description_full: Emerson Electric Co., a technology and software company, provides various solutions in the Americas, Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Europe. It operates through Final Control, Measurement & Analytical, Discrete Automation, Safety & Productivity, Control Systems & Software, and Test & Measurement segments. The Final Control segment provides control valves, isolation valves, shutoff valves, pressure relief valves, pressure safety valves, actuators, and regulators for process and hybrid industries under Anderson Greenwood, Bettis, Crosby, Fisher, Keystone, KTM, and Vanessa brands. The Measurement & Analytical segment supplies intelligent instrumentation measuring the physical properties of liquids or gases, such as pressure, temperature, level, flow, acoustics, corrosion, pH, conductivity, water quality, toxic gases, and flame under the Flexim, Micro Motion, and Rosemount brands. The Discrete Automation segment includes solenoid valves, pneumatic valves, valve position indicators, pneumatic cylinders and actuators, air preparation equipment, pressure and temperature switches, electric linear motion solutions, programmable automation control systems and software, electrical distribution equipment, and materials joining solutions used primarily in discrete industries under the Afag, Appleton, ASCO, Aventics, Branson, Movicon, PACSystems, SolaHD, TESCOM, and TopWorx brands. The Safety & Productivity segment delivers tools for professionals and homeowners that support infrastructure, promote safety, and enhance productivity under the Greenlee, Klauke, ProTeam, and RIDGID brands. The Control Systems & Software segment provides control systems and software that control plant processes by collecting and analyzing information from measurement devices in the plant under the DeltaV and Ovation brands. The Test & Measurement offers software-connected automated test and measurement systems. The company was incorporated in 1890 and is headquartered in Saint Louis, Missouri.

financial_summary: Emerson Electric Company is a large-cap industrials business with a $91.3B market cap on $19.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 42%.

The business throws off $3.5B in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.48× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.5× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn.

Shareholder yield of 2.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 18% operating margin runs 10pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

It accounts for 0.5% of sector revenue and 0.8% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-4.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 29% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 1.08, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $377.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash, 25% in the 2022 bear market and 56% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $84.13 (margin of safety -98%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $59.35 to $120 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 34.7 vs 24.1 and EV/EBITDA 16.9 vs 13.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 78% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 28 covering analysts target $183 on average, 10% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.33).
It runs a 42% gross margin and converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 9/9 and cash conversion of 1.48x.
ROE of 13% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
It spends 4.3% of revenue on R&D and 1.2% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.5x net debt to EBITDA ($1.8B of cash against $12.2B of debt), above the 1.5x gate.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.7, in the safe zone).
The current ratio of 0.94 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 43% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.8% over 3 years, 0.8% over 5 years and 2.7% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 3.4% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.05 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 51% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 2%.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (2.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 84%.
It returns 2.5% a year to shareholders (1.1% in buybacks and 1.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 53 consecutive years, raising it 0.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 70,000 employees, each generates about $271K of revenue, 0.7x the Industrials median.
That works out to $50K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.8M (21x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
